Follow a laser beam through an array of prisms, each of which turns the beam by its own angle, and list the prisms it hits in order.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/prism) (MIT). Listed under [Games & Simulation](/examples/?subject=games-and-simulation).

```nomi-run
// FILE: prism.nomi
//# Follows a laser beam through an array of prisms that turn it.

/// Where a laser beam is and the direction it travels in, in degrees
/// counterclockwise from the positive x axis.
pub struct Laser {
    x: Float
    y: Float
    angle: Float
}

/// A crystal at a point, which turns a beam that reaches it by `angle`
/// degrees.
pub struct Prism {
    id: Int
    x: Float
    y: Float
    angle: Float
}

/// How far a prism may sit off the beam's line, as a share of how far along
/// it the prism is, and still be hit: a thousandth of a radian.
once tolerance = 0.001

/// The ids of the prisms the beam from `start` hits, in order, until it
/// leaves the array.
//! prisms = [#Prism{id: 1, x: 10.0, y: 0.0, angle: 0.0}]
//! assert find_sequence(#{x: 0.0, y: 0.0, angle: 0.0}, prisms) == [1]
//
pub fn find_sequence(start: Laser, prisms: List<Prism>) -> List<Int> {
    trace(start, None, prisms, [])
}

/// The ids hit after `hits`, newest first, by `beam`, which leaves the prism
/// `from` or, at the start, none.
fn trace(beam: Laser, from: Maybe<Int>, prisms: List<Prism>, hits: List<Int>) -> List<Int> {
    case next_hit(beam, from, prisms) {
        None ->
            Iter.reverse(hits)

        Some(prism) -> {
            turned = #Laser{x: prism.x, y: prism.y, angle: beam.angle + prism.angle}
            trace(turned, Some(prism.id), prisms, [prism.id, ..hits])
        }
    }
}

/// The nearest prism ahead of `beam` on its line, other than the one it
/// leaves.
fn next_hit(beam: Laser, from: Maybe<Int>, prisms: List<Prism>) -> Maybe<Prism> {
    radians = beam.angle * Float.pi / 180.0
    across = Float.cos(radians)
    up = Float.sin(radians)

    prisms
    |> Iter.filter(fn prism -> Some(prism.id) != from)
    |> Iter.map(fn prism -> {
        dx = prism.x - beam.x
        dy = prism.y - beam.y
        #{prism, along: dx * across + dy * up, off: Float.abs(dx * up - dy * across)}
    })
    |> Iter.filter(fn hit -> hit.along > 0.0 and hit.off < hit.along * tolerance)
    |> Iter.min_by(.along)
    |> Maybe.map(.prism)
}
```

## How it's written

- The start is a `Laser`, a point and a direction in degrees, and each prism a struct of its id, point and turning angle, all `Float`s, so the canonical integers are written `10.0`.
- `trace` follows the beam with tail recursion: `next_hit` finds the nearest prism ahead, and the beam continues from that prism's point with the prism's angle added, until nothing is ahead. The beam never hits the prism it is leaving, which `from` names; it may come back to it later, as "same prism twice" does.
- `next_hit` projects each prism onto the beam's direction: `along` is how far ahead it lies and `off` how far beside the line. A prism is on the line when `off` is less than a thousandth of `along`, that is when the beam would miss it by under a thousandth of a radian. The canonical data states no tolerance; an exact test misses prisms in the two floating-point cases, where coordinates rounded to a tenth lie a little off the computed line, and a tolerance relative to the distance holds near and far prisms to the same angle.
- The 14 canonical cases are one `subtests` table named by the description column, each row a start, its prisms and the expected ids.
